title.en: Dangun Wanggeom: The Sandalwood King and the Founding of Gojoseon
title.zh: 檀君王儉：神檀樹之王與古朝鮮之建

region.zh: 韓國太白山／摩尼山（江原道）

texts.period: Recorded in Samguk Yusa (Iryeon, 1281, Book 1) citing the Weishu; principal editions: Haeinsa woodblock imprints (e.g. 1512); traditional foundation date 2333 BCE

source.work: Samguk Yusa, Book 1 (Dangun section), trans. Grafton K. Mintz and Tae-Hung Ha, Seoul 1972; Peter H. Lee, Sourcebook of Korean Civilization, New York 1993

texts.license: Ancient text public domain; Mintz & Ha 1972 quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Hwanin, lord of heaven, sends his son Hwanung to govern mankind from under the sandalwood tree on Taebaek mountain; a bear and a tiger wish to become human — only the bear endures the hundred days of mugwort and garlic and becomes the woman Ungnyeo; Hwanung marries her and she bears Dangun Wanggeom, who founds Gojoseon in 2333 BCE and rules 1,500 years before retiring as mountain god.
summary.zh: 天帝桓因遣子桓雄降於太白山神檀樹下，主理人間；熊與虎欲化為人——惟熊忍百日艾蒜之苦化為女子熊女；桓雄娶之，生檀君王儉；檀君於公元前2333年建古朝鮮，御世一千五百年，後隱為山神。

sensitivity.note: Living tradition: Dangun is venerated in Daejonggyo and used in national ideology (Gaecheonjeol); handle the nationalist reception critically.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Samguk Yusa I.1 (Mintz & Ha 1972): Hwanung, son of Hwanin, wished to descend and dwell in the human world; his father looked down and granted it, giving him three heavenly seals and 3,000 followers, and he alit under the sandalwood tree on Taebaek mountain and ruled the 360 human affairs — wind, rain, clouds, grain, life, disease, and punishment. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Samguk Yusa I.1 (Mintz & Ha 1972); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Samguk Yusa I.1 (ending): A bear and a tiger living in the same cave prayed to become human; Hwanung gave them mugwort and garlic, saying 'eat this, stay out of the sunlight for a hundred days, and you shall be human'; the tiger gave up, but the bear endured and became a woman; no husband offered himself, so she prayed under the sandalwood tree — and Hwanung made her his wife; she bore a son, Dangun Wanggeom. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Samguk Yusa I.1 (ending); not verbatim.

texts.language: Classical Chinese (Samguk Yusa's Korean historiographic Chinese)
texts.canonical_translation: Grafton K. Mintz and Tae-Hung Ha, Samguk Yusa: Legends and History of the Three Kingdoms, Seoul 1972 (copyright); Peter H. Lee, Sourcebook of Korean Civilization vol. 1, Columbia 1993 (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Dangun narrative is Korea's founding charter, recorded in the Samguk Yusa ('Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms'), compiled by the monk Iryeon in 1281, citing an earlier (lost) Wei shu source — the oldest extant full telling, some 1,200 years after the traditional founding date.

BEGINNING: HWANUNG'S DESCENT. Hwanin, the heavenly lord, has a son Hwanung who wishes to descend and benefit humankind. Hwanin looks over the world, finds it fit, grants his son the Three Heavenly Seals (the tokens of governance) and sends him down with 3,000 followers to the sandalwood tree (sindansu) on Taebaek mountain (identified with Mani-san on Ganghwa island or Taebaeksan in Gangwon). Hwanung rules under the tree as the 'Heavenly King', governing the 360 affairs of mankind: grain, life, disease, punishment — wind, rain, and clouds are his officers. Human society begins under the sandalwood tree — the 'sacred tree' that aitions both the name Dangun ('Sandalwood King') and the Korean reverence for mountain trees.

MIDDLE: THE BEAR AND THE TIGER. In the same cave live a bear and a tiger, who pray to Hwanung to become human. He gives them a bundle of mugwort and twenty-one cloves of garlic: 'eat this, shun the sunlight for a hundred days (twenty-one days in some tellings), and you shall take human form.' The tiger, wild and impatient, abandons the trial; the bear endures the fast in the dark cave, and after twenty-one days becomes a woman — Ungnyeo ('Bear Woman'). But no man will have her; she prays under the sandalwood tree for a child, and Hwanung — 'he changed himself into a man and married her' — fathers Dangun Wanggeom ('Sandalwood King'), born in the traditional year 2333 BCE.

END: THE FOUNDING AND THE RETIREMENT. Dangun founds the state of Joseon (Gojoseon, 'Old Joseon') at Asadal (identified variously with Pyongyang, a Liaodong site, or a mountain city) and rules 1,500 years. When King Ju of the Zhou enfeoffs Kija in the east (the Chinese dynastic tradition), Dangun retires — 'he hid himself and became the mountain god of Asadal' at 1,908 years of age: the founder abdicates into the landscape, becoming the mountain itself — the Korean pattern of the sacred mountain as ancestor. The Samguk Yusa closes the section with the Kija disclaimer, and the narrative anchors Korea's earliest history: Gojoseon's Bronze Age archaeology (Liaoning dolmens), the Dangun shrine on Ganghwa (Chamseongdan altar), the Daejonggyo religion (founded 1909, venerating Dangun), and the national holiday Gaecheonjeol ('Opening of Heaven Day', October 3).

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Korean identity (Dangun as common ancestor; the 'descendants of Dangun'), the theology of the sacred tree and mountain, the divine-origin charter of Korean kingship (used by Silla and Joseon dynasties), and the modern ideological uses — from Daejonggyo's veneration to Gaecheonjeol's state calendar — which scholarship reads critically alongside the myth's late manuscript date (1281) and its cited (lost) source.
narrative.zh: 《三國遺事》卷一記：天帝桓因子桓雄思降世人間，桓因俯察而許之，賜三枚天符印，率三千徒降於太白山神檀樹下，主穀、主命、主病、主刑等三百六十人間事——風雨雲皆其官。同穴之熊與虎願化人；桓雄賜艾與蒜：『食之，避陽光百日（一作二十一日），可得人形。』虎野而棄，熊忍而化為女子熊女；無男子肯娶，遂於神檀樹下祈子；桓雄化為人娶之，生檀君王儉（傳統紀年公元前2333年）。檀君建朝鮮（古朝鮮），都阿斯達，御世一千五百年；周封箕子於朝鮮後，檀君隱去，年一千九百零八歲為阿斯達山神——創始者歸於山，山即祖先。遺跡：江華島摩尼山塹城壇、大倧教（1909年建）、開天節（10月3日國定假日）。功能：韓民族認同之根、神樹與神山之信仰、王權神授憲章、以及現代意識形態之爭議使用（1281年成書晚、所引《魏書》已佚，學界批判性解讀）。

functions: Charter of Korean identity: Dangun as common ancestor ('descendants of Dangun')
Theology of the sacred tree and mountain: sindansu and Chamseongdan altar
Divine-origin kingship: charter used by later dynasties (Silla, Joseon)
Modern ideological uses: Daejonggyo religion and Gaecheonjeol (Oct. 3)

variants.name: Samguk Yusa version (1281)
variants.text_tradition: Iryeon, Book 1, citing the (lost) Weishu; Haeinsa imprints (1512)
variants.summary: The canonical telling: Hwanin-Hwanung-Dangun line, the bear-woman trial, Asadal, and the mountain-god retirement — the only full early text.

variants.name: Samguk Sagi silence (1145)
variants.summary: The court historian records Gojoseon and Kija but omits Dangun entirely — the Confucian canon's skepticism, a key datum in the historiographic debate.

variants.name: Dongui Bogam and later hagiography
variants.text_tradition: Joseon-era medical and religious texts; Daejonggyo liturgy (1909)
variants.summary: Dangun expands into herbalist-sage hagiographies (the trial's mugwort and garlic read as pharmacology) and the nationalist religion's liturgical cycle.

variants.name: Ganghwa archaeology
variants.text_tradition: Chamseongdan altar, Mani-san; dolmens of Gojoseon territory
variants.summary: The Ganghwa altar and the Liaodong-Korean dolmen belt are read by nationalists as Dangun's traces — archaeology as mythic evidence, debated.

title.en: Kaggen and the Eland: The San Creation of the Great Antelope
title.zh: 卡根與大羚羊：桑人創造大羚羊之敘事

region.en: Bushmanland / Katkop, Northern Cape, South Africa (Bleek-Lloyd archive region)
region.zh: 南非北開普布須曼地區／卡特科普（布里克-勞埃德檔案採錄區）

texts.period: Recorded 1870-84 by Wilhelm Bleek and Lucy Lloyd, Cape Town; informants named (Kabbo, Dia!kwain, A!kunta etc.); published Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore, London 1911

source.archive: Bleek and Lloyd Archive (University of Cape Town Libraries) / Internet Archive (Specimens 1911)
source.work: W. H. I. Bleek and L. C. Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore, London 1911 (public domain); D. F. Bleek, The Mantis and His Friends, 1923; archive: UCT Digital Collections

texts.license: Public domain (1911/1923 publications); archive materials with named informants (ethical publication practice established by Bleek & Lloyd)

summary.en: Kaggen, the trickster mantis, throws his sandal into the water and it becomes the first eland; he raises it like a child at the water-hole; when his brothers-in-law kill it for meat while he hunts honey, Kaggen grieves, transforms the eland's blood into new herds, and avenges the killing — the charter narrative of the eland's ritual centrality in San life and rock art.
summary.zh: 詭計者卡根（螳螂）將鞋擲入水中，化為第一頭大羚羊；如育幼兒般於水塘邊養之；其姻親趁其採蜜時獵殺取肉；卡根悲慟，化羚血為新群，並以詭計復仇——此為大羚羊在桑人生活與岩畫中儀式地位之憲章敘事。

sensitivity.note: Record uses the Bleek-Lloyd archive's named-informant publications (an ethical practice established in the 1870s-80s) and contemporary San organizations; rock art sites are sacred to San descendants.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Kabbo/Dia!kwain narrative (Bleek & Lloyd 1911): Kaggen took off his sandal, threw it into the water, and it became an eland; he kept it in his own place at the water-hole, fed it, and watched over it like a child — for the eland was Kaggen's beloved. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Kabbo/Dia!kwain narrative (Bleek & Lloyd 1911); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the killing narrative (Bleek & Lloyd 1911): While Kaggen was away getting honey, his brothers-in-law found the eland and killed it; Kaggen returned and wept; from the eland's blood and body more elands sprang up at the water-hole, so that the elands multiplied; and Kaggen, enraged, brought the hunters to harm — the first eland's death made both the herds and the danger. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the killing narrative (Bleek & Lloyd 1911); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore, 1911 (public domain); Lewis-Williams, Stories that Float from Afar, 2000 (copyright)

narrative.en:
The /Xam San narratives collected in the Bleek-Lloyd archive (1870-84, Cape Town, from named informants like Kabbo, Diakwain, and Akunta) preserve the richest body of San mythology. Kaggen (the Mantis) is the trickster-creator at its center.

BEGINNING: THE SANDAL BECOMES THE ELAND. Kaggen, walking with his family, takes off one of his sandals, throws it into the water, and it becomes the first eland — the great antelope of the Maluti/Drakensberg grasslands. He keeps it in his own place at the water-hole, hides it from the people (his brothers-in-law), and feeds and raises it 'like a child' — the eland is Kaggen's beloved, his foster-child and his heart's animal. (The narrative is at once an aition of the eland's origin and a portrait of Kaggen's ambivalence: the trickster whose love makes and unmakes.)

MIDDLE: THE KILLING. Kaggen goes off to hunt honey (or ostrich eggs); his brothers-in-law Cogaz and Kwammanga find the eland, drive it out, and kill it for meat. Kaggen returns, finds the blood and the kill, and weeps over his child: 'my eland!' — the death of the beloved animal is the myth's central grief. From the eland's blood and body (in the variants: the blood, the gall, the hooves) spring the elands of the world: the first death multiplies the herds — an aition of abundance through sacrifice.

END: THE TRICKSTER'S VENGEANCE AND THE RITUAL WORLD. Kaggen, enraged, takes revenge through trickery: he causes the hunters to be harmed (in the variants: he plants the poison grass, he sends the ants, he turns the game against them — the /Xam tellings vary) and withdraws from the people; the eland's parts are distributed with ritual consequence (the fat for the girls' puberty dances; eland hunting governed by the eland-bull dance). The narrative is the charter of the eland's centrality: San rock art (Drakensberg/Maluti panels) is dominated by eland imagery; the eland-bull dance (girls' puberty) and eland hunting rituals take their power from Kaggen's animal; and the trance dance's potency (n/um) is imagined as eland-like. The interpreter Kabbo told Bleek and Lloyd these stories in Cape Town's Breakwater Prison — the archive itself is the history of colonial incarceration and of ethical salvage (named informants, full interlinear translation).

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds San ritual ecology (the eland's ritual centrality; the puberty dance), the ethics of the trickster-creator (love, theft, and transformation as one), and the reading of rock art (Lewis-Williams's shamanic reading built on these narratives); it is also a founding document of San heritage politics — the archive's descendant communities now govern access and use.
narrative.zh: 布里克-勞埃德檔案（1870-84，開普敦）自具名報導人（Kabbo、Diakwain、Akunta 等）採錄 /Xam 桑人敘事，為桑人神話最富之存世文獻。卡根（螳螂）行路時脫下鞋擲入水中，化為首頭大羚羊；藏於水塘私處，餵養撫育『如子』——羚羊乃其所愛。卡根外出採蜜，其姻親（Cogaz 與 Kwammanga）尋得羚羊驅出而殺之取肉；卡根歸，見血與脂，哭其子：『我的羚羊！』——所愛之死為神話之核心悲劇。自羚之血與體（變體言血、膽、蹄）生出世上群羚：首死致萬羚，犧牲致豐饒之釋義。卡根怒而以詭計復仇（變體言投毒草、遣蟻群），離人而去；羚之部分以儀式分配（脂肪用於女子成年舞、獵羚受羚牛舞之約束）。此敘事為大羚羊儀式中心地位之憲章：德拉肯斯堡岩畫以羚為主，成年禮舞與獵羚儀式皆源自卡根之獸，入迷舞之力（n/um）亦想像如羚。報導人 Kabbo 於開普敦碼頭監獄向布里克與勞埃德講述——檔案本身即殖民監禁史與倫理搶救（具名報導人、逐行對譯）之歷史。功能：儀式生態、詭計創造者之倫理、岩畫釋讀之據；檔案後裔社群現掌其使用與取用之權。

functions: Charter of the eland's ritual centrality in San life and rock art
Eland-bull dance and girls' puberty ritual grounded in the narrative
Trickster-creator ethics: love, theft, and transformation as one act
Rock art interpretation: Lewis-Williams's shamanic reading built on these texts

variants.name: Bleek & Lloyd archive versions (Kabbo, Diakwain, Akunta)
variants.text_tradition: 1870-84 recordings, Cape Town; published Specimens (1911) and The Mantis and His Friends (1923)
variants.summary: The richest family: multiple named-informant tellings with interlinear /Xam-English; differences in how the eland multiplies and how Kaggen takes revenge.

variants.name: Maluti/Drakensberg rock art panel readings
variants.summary: The painted corpus interprets Kaggen's eland as the trance-animal of potency — the narrative read against the rock art (and vice versa), the central method of San studies.

variants.name: Khomani and Kalahari San tellings
variants.text_tradition: 20th-c. Kalahari recordings (Khomani land claims materials; Guenther's G/wi and //Gana work)
variants.summary: Northern San traditions preserve Kaggen-type tricksters with different animal foci — the living Kalahari stratum against the archived /Xam.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The Bleek-Lloyd archive's named-informant practice (1870s-80s) remains the ethical benchmark for citation; descendant San communities (San Institute of Southern Africa; Khomani communities) govern heritage use. Rock art sites are sacred; summarize, do not reproduce restricted ritual detail; prefer contemporary San-authored scholarship.
